title: First preview of DialogueCraft, a dialogue manager and generator that is tailor made for game devs
author: MoneySquirrel1910
selftext:
Hi! This is an early preview of a web-app I'm working on called DialogueCraft, which I intend to release in the coming days.

All voiceovers you hear in the video are generated directly through DialogueCraft on the browser.

Write your dialogues in the app and generate high-quality voiceovers for them in seconds with just a single click. Bring your in-game characters directly into the app and assign a unique and high quality voice to them. DialogueCraft offers 180 voices to choose from, ranging from humans, monsters, robots and more!

I'm a game developer myself and while I was developing my game, which contains many lines of dialogue, I was looking up all the TTS tools on the Internet. I found many great tools out there that were capable of generating high-quality audio for my written dialogue, but I found that they were all VERY inconvenient for game development for a multitude of reasons: 

* There was no real way to organize scenes and set up a proper structure just like you would have it inside your game engine. You can't really see a visual representation of the flow of your dialogue, especially if you have multiple characters.
* There's no way to bring your in-game characters into the tools, which makes the disconnection between your written dialogue and the voiceover for it even greater.
* If you've generated audio for a long dialogue scene, making a small edit will require you to regenerate the full audio for the entire scene. This quickly becomes very costly and time-consuming.
* Downloaded audio files followed generic names ("voice\_line\_1"). This becomes unbearable when you have hundreds or thousands of individual voice lines and having to manually edit the name of each file.

I developed DialogueCraft to address all those issues and to create the best dialogue voiceover generation tool for game developers.

I am very open to hear your feedback and to answer any questions you have!

If you want to receive a reminder when the app launches, send me a DM.

comments.author: surpurdurd
comments.body: I'd be interested in trying this. How much of the inference being done is local vs cloud based? How do you plan on charging? What (if anything) do you plan on letting people try for free?

replies.author: MoneySquirrel1910
replies.body: The voice synthesis is done through the ElevenLabs text-to-speech API so it is entirely through the cloud. I will charge with a monthly subscription and there will be a free plan which gives 5000 free credits which is the equivalent of generating around 10 minutes of audio time. Apart from some download restrictions, the free plan will give all the same features as the paid plan. Hope that answers your questions :)

replies.author: Other-Football72
replies.body: You go through ElevnLabs w/ this, or it's done separately by the user?

replies.author: MoneySquirrel1910
replies.body: Currently it is set up with my own ElevenLabs api key, so new users do not require their own ElevenLabs account or subscription.

comments.author: Sleepnotdeading
comments.body: TBH the performances sound pretty bad.  As a player, I would be slamming the skip button to get through the dialogue.  Sounds like what you've got is a wrapper for some basic ElevenLabs API calls and a bulk file renamer.  Why are you planning to charge a subscription for that?  Why not just let people bring their own elevenlabs API keys?  I could see this being useful if it was an integrated feature in a full script writing software that let you, after writing a scene, hit a button and generate temp line-readings.  As it is, I fail to see how this is better than just using elevenlabs directly and power renamer to get the files named how I want.

replies.author: MoneySquirrel1910
replies.body:
There's not much I can do about the voiceover performances since that's just the current state of quality that AI TTS tools can offer. It uses the ElevenLabs V3 model which is pretty much the best AI TTS model currently available. I would like to say though that the audio you hear on the preview video would probably have sounded better with some better prompt engineering and by following some of the guidelines on [Best practices | ElevenLabs Documentation](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/overview/capabilities/text-to-speech/best-practices). Of course the quality will NEVER be as good as hiring a professional voice actor but personally I think the voiceovers sound good enough and I have definitely seen many mega-successful games out there which have used FAR worse voiceovers.

***"Sounds like what you've got is a wrapper for some basic ElevenLabs API calls and a bulk file renamer."***

Not at all. As I wrote in the title, DialogueCraft is a dialogue manager and generator, and not just ElevenLabs wrapped in another interface. The main purpose of the app is to serve as a place where you write your dialogue scripts, organized into projects, scenes and individual lines, and then generate voicelines for your audio either line-by-line or all at once with just a single click. You can tweak and edit each line without ruining the entire flow of your dialogues. When you are done, you can choose naming options and conventions for the filenames and download all lines in bulk, structured into folders for scenes and filenames which can include character name, line number, line title etc... (e.g. line\_1\_john\_says\_hi.mp3). Doing this manually can be very tedious, even with bulk renamers. Also the renaming issue is just one of the many problems with current TTS tools that DialogueCraft aims to solve. There are other problems aswell which I mentioned in the post.

***"I could see this being useful if it was an integrated feature in a full script writing software that let you, after writing a scene, hit a button and generate temp line-readings."***

That's exactly what DialogueCraft is.

***"Why not just let people bring their own elevenlabs API keys?"***

This was something I highly considered during development, but after doing some research on the "bring your own key" (BYOK) model I decided in the end to not do it. Most BYOK apps are not successful because people usually do not want to go through additional steps to set up the app. Also in this case the BYOK model would not necessarily mean that the users would save money by it, since the cheapest ElevenLabs plan only gives 10 custom voice slots, whereas ALL plans in DialogueCraft, even the free one, gives 160 custom voice slots and many other benefits that users would otherwise have to pay hefty sums to get directly from ElevenLabs. 

***"I fail to see how this is better than just using elevenlabs directly and power renamer to get the files named how I want."***

Yes you can save some money by using ElevenLabs directly and manually organize your files and dialogue scripts. DialogueCraft is just intended as a quality of life tool that speeds up and brings some organization and structure to your game dialogue TTS workflows. To draw a parallel, it's just like how people use paid planning tools like Notion instead of just using something simple and completely free like Google Docs.

replies.author: Sleepnotdeading
replies.body:
I guess I don’t get it.  The quality isn’t shippable, so it’s useful for temp at best.  I can do all this in eleven labs with full control via a tiny bit of python and some API calls, or a rough and fast version of this using just their browser tools.  Since I’m not going to write my script in your app, I’d have to re-write my script in your app… which is just using those same api calls and text markups anyway. 

I’m not trying to be a downer, but for me to seriously consider a tool it has to save me time, save me money, or improve quality.

replies.author: MoneySquirrel1910
replies.body:
I understand, your criticism is very fair.

Just out of curiosity, have you used ElevenLabs yourself for dialogues in game development?

replies.author: Sleepnotdeading
replies.body:
Yes, my prior studio integrated elevenlabs as part of the process of importing the script into Unreal.  At import, all dialogue lines were assigned unique filenames, and the text of those lines would be sent to elevenlabs via API calls for generation.  The returned audio files would be assigned the correct filenames and would auto-populate the appropriate Unreal sequences created by the import process.  Character models and props were also auto-populated, and eventually cameras and lights as well.  The goal was to push a button in our script software, and get a t-pose theatre MVP version of the level and its cinematics in Unreal.  When the mocap was eventually shot and processed, it would overwrite the temp stuff.

We were dealing with dozens of scenes, hundreds of sequences, and thousands of lines, so that workflow is probably over-engineered for small indie games.  For my money though, the only way elevenlabs dialogue approaches shippable is with their speech-to-speech transformation.  I'd love a workflow where I could record all the lines myself (or hire one or two VO actors to voice a whole cast) and then send them off to be transformed via API calls, but last I checked for this feature (which was admittedly a while ago) it still didn't exist outside of browser tools.

replies.author: MoneySquirrel1910
replies.body:
Thank you for a very detailed response. It sounds like you had a very sophisticated framework set up in your previous studio :)

I had not read up on ElevenLabs speech-to-speech tool but it sounds like something I could integrate into my app. I will definitely dig into it more.

Thanks again!

replies.body: I appreciate it! I will get in contact through dm once Im ready to do early testing.
